# FamilySearch Wiki: United States census records for tracing a family

United States federal census records are among the most important genealogical sources. A census was taken every ten years beginning in 1790. FamilySearch has a census collection with an index and images for each federal census year from 1790 through 1950. Most of these censuses are also on subscription sites such as Ancestry, Findmypast, and MyHeritage, which require a paid subscription for full access. To search census records, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, enter your ancestor's name, and filter by record type 'Census, Voter Lists.' What a census recorded about each household member changed over time: from 1790 through 1840, only the head of household is named, and everyone else is counted only as tally marks within age and sex categories; from 1850 through 1870, every free person in the household is listed by name with age, sex, and birthplace, but relationship to the head of household is not stated; beginning in 1880, every person is listed by name together with their relationship to the head of household.

By tracing a family through multiple census years, you can watch children grow up, track a family's migration, and identify previously unknown relatives. Each census decade can point you to a new location or a maiden name. When searching, try alternate spellings of surnames and consider that ages reported in different census years may vary by several years.

## Sources

- [United States Census — Background](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Background)
- [United States Census — Strategy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Strategy)

args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Irish church records

Church records are among the most important sources for Irish genealogy research. The two main denominations that kept parish registers in Ireland were the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland (Anglican). Roman Catholic registers generally begin in the early 1800s, while Church of Ireland registers often start earlier, in the 1700s. Many original registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire, but microfilmed copies and transcriptions survive. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large collection of Irish Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers, which are freely searchable at FamilySearch.org. To find Irish church records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org and click Search, then Records. Enter your ancestor's name and select Ireland as the country. Filter results by record type to narrow to church records including baptisms, marriages, and burials. The National Library of Ireland also holds a large collection of Catholic parish registers on microfilm, many of which have been digitized and are available online. The Representative Church Body Library in Dublin holds Church of Ireland registers not destroyed in 1922. Irish church records typically contain baptism (christening) records listing the child's name, baptism date, parents' names, and sometimes the townland or parish of residence. Marriage records list the names of the bride and groom, the date and place of marriage, and witnesses. Burial records list the name of the deceased and the burial date. Earlier records may contain less detail. Some registers also include sponsor names for baptisms, which can help identify other family members.

## Sources

- [Ireland Church Records - Overview of Irish Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Overview_of_Irish_Church_Records)
- [Ireland Church Records - Finding Church Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Finding_Church_Records_on_FamilySearch)

**Finding 1800s Death Records – FamilySearch Wiki Guidance**

The wiki pages on **United States Death Records** and **Pennsylvania Vital Records** (as a regional example) provided the following key points:

1. **Civil Registration was not universal in the 1800s.** Most U.S. states did not require mandatory death registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s. Coverage varies widely by state and county.

2. **Key record types to search for 1800s deaths:**
   - **Cemetery and gravestone records** – Often the most reliable source for pre-registration deaths
   - **Church burial registers** – Many congregations kept death/burial records before civil registration began
   - **Obituaries and newspapers** – Local newspapers published death notices; check digitized newspaper archives
   - **Probate/estate records** – Filed when someone died with property; often include death date and family details
   - **Census mortality schedules** – The 1850–1880 federal censuses included a mortality schedule listing people who died in the year prior to the census
   - **Death certificates** – Available in some states from the 1860s–1880s onward, though many states started later
   - **Bible records and family papers** – Family Bibles often recorded deaths

3. **Where to search on FamilySearch:**
   - Search [FamilySearch Records](https://www.familysearch.org/search/records) by name, death year, and place
   - Browse digitized collections by state/county under the FamilySearch catalog
   - Check the **Vital Records** and **Cemetery Records** collections for the relevant state

4. **State-specific resources:** Each state has its own wiki page on FamilySearch detailing when death registration began and what records survive.

The guidance has been saved to your research log. You can now use this to plan your specific search for your ancestor's death record.

# FamilySearch Wiki: death records for someone who died in the 1800s

For deaths in the mid-to-late 1800s, researchers should check death certificates (where available), church burial registers, cemetery records, obituaries in local newspapers, and probate records. Statewide death registration in the United States typically began between 1880 and 1920 depending on the state. FamilySearch has collections of early death records from many states and counties. To find death records on FamilySearch, go to the Search tab and select Records, enter the ancestor's name, and narrow by country, state, and date range. The FamilySearch catalog lists available collections; select a state and look under Vital Records. Some collections are indexed and fully searchable; others are browse-only and require reviewing images page by page. Pennsylvania began statewide civil registration of deaths in 1906; before that, death records are found at the county or municipal level and survive unevenly.

## Sources

- [United States Death Records — Early Death Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Death_Records#Early_Death_Records)
- [United States Death Records — Searching Death Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Death_Records#Searching_Death_Records_on_FamilySearch)
- [Pennsylvania Vital Records — Death Certificates (1906–present)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records#Death_Records)

args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: German church records

Church records (Kirchenbücher) are the most important source for German genealogy before civil registration. Protestant (Evangelisch) and Catholic (Katholisch) parishes recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials, with many registers beginning in the 1600s and some Catholic registers reaching back to the mid-1500s. Each register is kept by the parish, not by the town, so identifying the correct parish is the essential first step.

To find the parish that served an ancestor's village, use a gazetteer. Meyers Orts- und Verkehrs-Lexikon des Deutschen Reichs lists every place in the 1871-1918 German Empire and identifies the civil registration office and the Protestant and Catholic parishes serving it.

Many German church records have been microfilmed or digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog under the parish or town name. Others remain only at the parish, the regional church archive (Landeskirchliches Archiv or Kirchenbuchamt), or on subscription sites such as Archion (Protestant) and Matricula (Catholic).

## Sources

- [Germany Church Records — Getting Started](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records#Getting_Started)
- [Germany Gazetteers — Meyers Gazetteer](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Gazetteers#Meyers_Gazetteer)
- [Germany Church Records — Where to Find the Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records#Where_to_Find_the_Records)

ops.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Immigration records

Immigration records document the arrival of individuals into a country and are a key source for tracing ancestors who moved from one country to another. For the United States, passenger arrival records (also called ship manifests or passenger lists) are the primary immigration records. These records were created at the port of arrival and typically list the passenger's name, age, occupation, country of origin, and destination. FamilySearch has a large free collection of U.S. passenger arrival records searchable by name at FamilySearch.org.

To find immigration records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, and enter your ancestor's name. You can filter by record type and country of origin to narrow results. Naturalization records are also useful, as they document the process by which an immigrant became a citizen and may include the immigrant's country of birth, arrival date, and port of entry. Naturalization records were kept at the local court level and FamilySearch has indexed many of them.

## Sources

- [United States Immigration Records — Overview of Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Immigration_Records#Overview_of_Immigration_Records)
- [United States Immigration Records — Finding Immigration Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Immigration_Records#Finding_Immigration_Records_on_FamilySearch)

## Finding Land Records for Pennsylvania Ancestors

The FamilySearch Wiki covers Pennsylvania land records in detail. Key points from the guidance:

### Types of Land Records Available

- **Patent Records** – After the survey, a patent (deed from the Commonwealth) was issued granting legal title.
- **Deed Books** – Once land changed hands between private parties, deeds were recorded at the county level.

### Where Records Are Held
- **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** – Holds the original warrant and patent records (pre-1809 records are largely digitized on FamilySearch).

1. Identify the **county** where your ancestor lived — land records are county-level after the initial patent stage.
2. Search FamilySearch for the collection *Pennsylvania Land Records, 1699–1879*.

4. For deeds, check the county Recorder of Deeds, many of which have been microfilmed and are available on FamilySearch.

# FamilySearch Wiki: probate or will records for a deceased ancestor

Probate records are created when a deceased person's estate is settled through a court process. They include wills, inventories of property, letters of administration, and final settlements. Probate records can identify family members (especially heirs), provide an economic snapshot, and confirm dates and places. In the United States, probate is handled at the county level; records are held by county probate courts or surrogate courts. FamilySearch has indexed and digitized probate records from many counties across the country. To find probate records on FamilySearch, search the FamilySearch Catalog by state and county under the 'Probate records' category. Many collections are browse-only images. When a will is found, read it carefully, as testators often name children, grandchildren, and in-laws by name. Intestate records (for those who died without a will) list heirs and their relationships to the deceased, which can be equally valuable for establishing family connections.

- [United States Probate Records — What Are Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#What_Are_Probate_Records)
- [United States Probate Records — Finding Probate Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#Finding_Probate_Records_on_FamilySearch)
